en.title: You Paid for a Service but Did Not Receive It
en.directAnswer: Keep the contract, advertisement, invoice, payment proof and promised service date. Ask the provider in writing to perform the service or explain the refund position. The Consumers’ Right Protection Act includes provisions relating to promised goods or services, but the correct remedy depends on the facts and the service.

atAGlance.whoFor: A consumer paid for a promised service that was not provided.
atAGlance.legalBasis: Consumers’ Right Protection Act, 2009, including provisions on promised goods/services; DNCRP process.
atAGlance.mainRule: Do not promise a refund in every case. Contract terms and the law both matter.
atAGlance.updateStatus: Verify the exact complaint deadline and DNCRP jurisdiction before publication.

en.lawMeaning: Do not promise a refund in every case. Contract terms and the law both matter. This page gives a general route. A person’s exact rights can change because of facts, documents, deadlines, legal status, court orders or later amendments.
steps: Escalate through the correct consumer or sector route.
evidence: Contract; invoice; receipt; ad; email/chat; schedule; cancellation terms; payment proof.
en.simpleExample: A training company cancels a paid course and offers no new date. Students should save the course advertisement and payment receipt before asking for a refund.
commonMistakes: Common mistakes: Relying on phone calls only.
Common mistakes: accepting a different service without written agreement.
Common mistakes: making public accusations before facts are clear..
